analysis.one_liner: Bans new offshore oil and gas leasing off Florida and cancels existing leases with federal compensation.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan group of Florida House members, 7 Democrats and 7 Republicans among the cosponsors, backed a ban on offshore drilling off their state, but the bill died in House committee without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have barred the Interior Department from holding any new oil and gas lease sales or issuing new leases in the federal waters off Florida's coasts, from the Alabama line to the Georgia line. It would also have ordered the cancellation of every existing lease in the eastern Gulf of Mexico south of 26 degrees north latitude, with any compensation owed to leaseholders paid by the U.S. Treasury rather than by Florida. Before any drilling could resume after 2002, the Interior Department would have had to complete extensive environmental and oceanographic studies reviewed by independent scientists, and Congress would have received annual reports on the lease cancellations.
analysis.who_benefits: Florida's coastal communities, tourism businesses, and fishing interests gain protection from offshore drilling risks such as spills. Florida residents and beach-dependent economies would bear no cost, since any compensation to canceled leaseholders would come from the federal Treasury. Federal waters off Florida would stay off-limits to new drilling at least until January 1, 2002, and possibly longer if required studies were not finished.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits the Interior Secretary from conducting lease sales or issuing any new oil and gas leases in the outer continental shelf off Florida, between the Florida-Alabama and Florida-Georgia seaward boundaries, until at least January 1, 2002.

Requires cancellation of all existing federal leases south of 26 degrees north latitude and east of 86 degrees west longitude — the eastern Gulf of Mexico off Florida — with annual reports to Congress on the cancellations until complete.

Before drilling could be reconsidered, the Secretary would have to complete ecological, socioeconomic, oceanographic, and endangered-species studies, each reviewed by at least three independent scientists nominated by the Florida Academy of Sciences and approved by both the Secretary and Florida's Governor.
Any compensation owed to canceled leaseholders would be paid from the U.S. Treasury, and Florida would incur no cost or liability from the cancellations.

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas companies holding leases in the eastern Gulf lose their leases, with compensation paid out of the U.S. Treasury — meaning federal taxpayers as a whole pick up the cancellation costs. The federal government also forgoes potential lease sale revenue, and authorizes up to $1 million a year for eight fiscal years to fund the required studies.

drawbacks.text: Canceling existing leases would require the federal government to compensate the leaseholders out of the U.S. Treasury, putting the bill's cost on taxpayers nationwide rather than on Florida alone.
Removing a large area of federal waters from drilling eliminates potential federal oil and gas lease revenue and could reduce domestic energy production, a cost an honest supporter would acknowledge.
The bill authorizes $1 million per year for eight fiscal years for environmental and oceanographic studies, a new federal expense layered on top of the cancellation costs.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For Florida's coastal economy and environment the protection is substantial and the state bears none of the cost directly. The trade-off is real but narrow: taxpayers nationwide would pay leaseholder compensation and study funding, and the country forgoes drilling in one region's federal waters. On balance the benefits to coastal residents and industries outweigh the diffuse federal costs, though the Treasury-funded compensation makes the bill more expensive than a simple leasing ban.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to two House committees and then to subcommittees, where it sat until the 103rd Congress ended without any vote.

narrative.text: Porter Goss of Florida introduced the bill on January 26, 1993, joined by eleven fellow Florida House members, and it drew 14 cosponsors split evenly between Democrats and Republicans.

The bill was referred jointly to the House Committees on Natural Resources and Merchant Marine and Fisheries, and in February 1993 to subcommittees on Oceanography, Gulf of Mexico, and the Outer Continental Shelf and on Energy and Mineral Resources.
The Interior Department was asked for its comments, but no committee ever reported the bill, no vote was ever taken, and the Congress ended on January 3, 1995 with the bill still in committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas leaseholders in the eastern Gulf of Mexico are better off, since their leases were never canceled and no compensation was ever owed. Federal taxpayers also avoided the cancellation costs, and drilling in the region remained possible under existing law.

for.name: Rep. Porter Goss
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led the effort to ban drilling and cancel leases off Florida.

for.name: 14 House cosponsors
for.role: 14 cosponsors (7 Democrats, 7 Republicans), including the Florida members named in the bill's introduction
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, split evenly between the two parties.

against.name: House Natural Resources and Merchant Marine and Fisheries Committees
against.role: Committees to which the bill was jointly referred
against.what_they_did: Never reported the bill out of committee or scheduled it for a vote during the 103rd Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Support was bipartisan from the start: the 14 cosponsors split 7 Democrats and 7 Republicans, and 12 Florida House members of both parties joined the introduction.

industries.note: The bill cancels their existing eastern Gulf leases, blocks any new leasing off Florida, and pays them compensation from the Treasury. Their interest in drilling the region runs against the coastal protection ordinary Floridians would get from the ban.

Keeping drilling out of Florida's federal waters protects beaches, fisheries, and the tourism economy from spill risk. The bill puts Florida residents' interests alongside these industries rather than charging the state anything for the protection.
